name: CARD9 deficiency
aliases: caspase recruitment domain family member 9 deficiency
inherited susceptibility to invasive fungal disease

clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive defect in the adaptor protein that transmits fungal-recognition signals from C-type lectin receptors, producing a selective vulnerability to fungal infection in otherwise healthy people

The signature phenotype is invasive and often central-nervous-system fungal disease, including candida meningoencephalitis, which is unusual because candidal infection spares the brain in most other immunodeficiencies
Deep dermatophytosis with extensive skin, nail, and lymph-node invasion by ordinary tinea organisms is a characteristic presentation
Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, invasive candidiasis without a central venous catheter, and infections with dematiaceous (pigmented) moulds also occur
Bacterial and viral infections are typically not a feature, which helps distinguish this from broader combined immunodeficiencies
Diagnosis combines the distinctive fungal phenotype with reduced interleukin-17-producing T cells and confirmatory genetic testing
Management relies on prolonged, sometimes lifelong antifungal therapy, with adjunctive immunomodulation considered in refractory central-nervous-system disease
reference.pathophysiology: CARD9 is a cytoplasmic adaptor that couples fungal-sensing C-type lectin receptors, such as those recognising beta-glucans and mannans on fungal walls, to downstream signalling in myeloid cells. When a phagocyte detects a fungus, these receptors normally activate CARD9, which assembles a signalling complex that switches on nuclear factor kappa B and drives production of cytokines needed for neutrophil recruitment and for the development of interleukin-17-producing T cells that protect skin and mucosa. Loss of CARD9 uncouples fungal recognition from this response, so neutrophils are poorly mobilised to fungal foci (notably in the central nervous system) and the antifungal interleukin-17 axis is impaired, allowing candida, dermatophytes, and pigmented moulds to invade tissues that they would not ordinarily penetrate.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic granulomatous disease with fungal infection
Acquired immunosuppression or HIV with invasive fungal disease
additionalInvestigations: Enumeration of circulating interleukin-17-producing T-helper cells
Functional assays of cytokine production by monocytes after fungal or lectin-receptor stimulation
Fungal culture and histology from affected sites with species identification
Neuroimaging and cerebrospinal fluid analysis when central-nervous-system disease is suspected
Beta-glucan and other fungal antigen or serological markers
Exclusion of HIV and other acquired immunodeficiency
redFlags: Candida or other fungal infection of the central nervous system in an apparently immunocompetent host
Deep, invasive dermatophytosis extending beyond the skin
Invasive candidiasis in the absence of usual risk factors such as a central line
Infection with dematiaceous moulds causing brain abscess
Progressive fungal disease despite adequate first-line antifungal therapy
reference.prognosis: With prolonged antifungal treatment many patients are controlled, but central-nervous-system fungal disease carries appreciable morbidity and mortality, relapse is frequent, and lifelong surveillance or suppressive therapy is often required.
pitfalls: Attributing central-nervous-system candidiasis to an unusual exposure rather than a host defect, since it is rare in immunocompetent people
Undertreating deep dermatophytosis as if it were superficial tinea
Assuming a normal routine immune workup excludes the disorder, as antibody and lymphocyte counts are usually normal
Discontinuing antifungals too soon and provoking relapse
Missing the diagnosis in adults, in whom presentation may be delayed
references: Stiehm's Immunologic Disorders in Infants and Children
IUIS Expert Committee classification of inborn errors of immunity
